overview: American Samoa is a United States territory in the eastern Samoan archipelago, with a cultural history much older than that political relationship. Basalt quarries, siapo barkcloth, schools and government records illuminate skilled work, community life and changing authority. Its history is connected with, but politically distinct from, the independent state of Samoa.

periods.title: Naval administration
periods.summary: US naval administration began in 1900. The Tutuila and Aunu'u deed was signed that year; the Manu'a deed followed in 1904. These were distinct documents within a wider history of foreign partition and Samoan negotiation.

periods.title: Civilian administration and local institutions
periods.summary: Administration transferred to the US Department of the Interior in July 1951. A revised constitution in 1967 and the first election of a governor in 1977 marked later changes within the continuing territorial relationship.

items.text: Tutuila's Tataga-matau quarry above Leone formed part of a wider landscape of basalt extraction and tool making. Te Rangi Hiroa investigated it in 1927 with information from village elders. Quarry research combines physical remains with knowledge retained by local communities.

A 2007 study analyzed geological samples from four Tutuila quarries and distinguished their chemical signatures. This supplies a way to test where a stone tool originated. It does not, by itself, date a tool or identify the person who carried it between islands.

Hamilton Library in Hawaii holds a siapo mamanu made by Mary Pritchard around 1965, using mulberry bark and organic dyes. A named artist and a dated work make it possible to follow a particular contribution to Samoan art instead of treating every cloth as anonymous tradition.

Siapo makers soften bark, scrape it with shells and beat it on a wooden anvil. Joining sheets creates larger surfaces for decoration. Pattern-board printing and freehand mamanu painting offer different ways to arrange designs, with hand finishing allowing variation between repeated forms.

Pritchard recalled learning in Leone from Kolone Fai'ivae Leoso and other women while helping cultivate and harvest paper mulberry. Her account links artistic training to gardening, preparation, conversation and shared work, rather than only the final painted surface.

Pritchard also described exporting siapo and adapting designs to shirts, dresses and household cloth. Those recollections show artists responding to markets while teaching and sustaining their practice. Innovation and cultural continuity could be parts of the same working life.

An umu uses heated stones and layers of leaves to cook food for family gatherings. Taro, breadfruit, fish and other ingredients can share the cooking space. Preparing such a meal joins knowledge of heat, plant materials and timing with cooperative work.

Palusami combines taro leaves with coconut cream, wrapped and cooked until tender. The dish makes two cultivated plants central to a shared meal, alongside other foods that vary with the household and occasion.

Atauloma Girls School on Tutuila opened in 1900 through the London Missionary Society, with funds raised by Samoan residents. Classrooms and dormitories made formal schooling possible away from home, while its preparation of future pastors' wives reflected a particular religious and gendered purpose.

The National Park Service's 1993 lease included village-owned land managed through the matai system. A later Traditional Use Study documented knowledge of plants, marine resources and culturally important places. Continuing local access is part of maintaining that knowledge.

The 1900 Tutuila and Aunu'u deed transferred sovereignty while promising protection of land and property and qualified retention of chiefly control of towns. Its clauses reveal which powers and protections were being negotiated; the document alone cannot represent every resident's view.

The Manu'a deed of 1904 was signed by Tuimanu'a and island chiefs. American Samoa's archives emphasize his annotation concerning equality and tradition. The territorial commission later stressed that US authority had already been proclaimed before the cessions, complicating a simple story of voluntary transfer.

President Truman's executive order transferred administration from the Navy to the Interior Department effective 1 July 1951. Voters first elected a governor in 1977. These changes concerned how the territory was governed, while Samoan family and village institutions continued.

ending.text: American Samoa continues as a US territory. Naval government ended in 1951, and later constitutional and electoral changes expanded local political institutions. Those transitions did not end Samoan communities, language, chiefly relationships or artistic practice, nor did they unite the territory politically with independent Samoa.
